key_terms.meaning: A set of independent computers that cooperate over a network and appear to users as a single coherent system.
Hidden properties: users do not see that several machines work in parallel, or that one of them has failed and been replaced.
One node or link fails while the rest keep running, so a program must detect and tolerate a failure it cannot see directly.
Data transfer between processes that share no memory, done by explicit send and receive operations over a channel.
A blocking send waits until the receiver or buffer accepts the message; a non-blocking send returns at once and the buffer holds the data.
Converting arguments into a flat byte sequence (with a fixed data representation) so they survive the trip across the network.
Small local procedures that pack arguments, send the request, wait, and unpack the reply, so the call looks local to the programmer.
The call is retried after a timeout, so the server may execute the operation more than once; safe only if the operation is idempotent.
An atomic action of a process, either an internal step, a send of a message, or a receive of a message; it has no duration in the model.
No bound on message delay or relative process speed; only the order of events along each process and on each channel is known.
The instantaneous difference between two clocks, or between a clock and the reference time.
The rate at which a clock gains or loses time against a reference, usually a few parts per million for a quartz crystal.
The distance of an NTP server from the reference clock; stratum 1 servers are directly attached, stratum 2 servers sync from stratum 1, and so on.
a causally precedes b if a and b are on the same process with a earlier, or a is the send of the message b receives, or the relation chains through such steps.
One integer C per process; rule C(b) = max(C(a), C(msg)) + 1 on each event, so a → b implies C(a) < C(b) but not the reverse.
An array of n counters, one per process, giving each process's knowledge of how many events have occurred at every process; V(a) < V(b) if and only if a → b.
Neither a → b nor b → a; with vector clocks this holds exactly when neither vector is less than or equal to the other.
A set of local states plus the messages in transit such that every message received is also recorded as sent, and no received message is missing.
A control message sent on each incoming channel to tell a process to record its state and start recording messages on that channel.
A promise that all correct members of a group deliver all messages in the same sequence, whatever the senders' timing.

takeaways: A distributed system trades the simplicity of shared memory for independence and scale, so every design problem reduces to coping with no global clock, no shared memory and partial failure.
Processes without common memory can only exchange explicit messages, and the design lives in the exact rules for send, receive, buffering and blocking.
Remote procedure call hides the message behind a local-looking stub, and its real difficulties are marshalling, failure detection and repeated execution.
The asynchronous model assumes no bound on delay, so algorithms must be correct under any interleaving; the synchronous model buys simplicity by assuming known time bounds.
Physical clocks drift, so NTP keeps them within a stated bound of UTC by comparing with servers at a known stratum and adjusting rate as well as offset.
Lamport's happened-before relation is the correct notion of causal order; a scalar counter respects it but cannot detect concurrency.
A vector clock is exactly equivalent to happened-before, so it can tell apart causal order from concurrent events at the cost of n counters per timestamp.
A snapshot taken by recording local states independently may be inconsistent; the Chandy-Lamport marker algorithm on FIFO channels gives a consistent one without stopping anything.
Group communication strengthens ordering step by step: FIFO keeps a single sender's order, causal adds happens-before, total forces one common order and also solves mutual exclusion.
Mutual exclusion, leader election and termination detection all reduce to ordering events or agreeing on a common global state.
bank_note: Long answers are expected to prove properties, not just describe them: state the system model, give the algorithm, prove the safety property (mutual exclusion, consistency of the snapshot, causal delivery), then argue complexity in number of messages and time delay.

bank.q: Define a distributed system and explain the design challenges that arise from having no shared memory, no global clock and only partial failure. Give one Indian application example for each challenge.
outline: Definition: independent computers cooperating to appear as one system
Heterogeneity: different hardware, operating systems and languages must interoperate
No global clock: each node has its own crystal, so ordering needs logical clocks or NTP bounds
No shared memory: communication is by messages only, so latency and loss must be handled
Partial failure: a node or link dies while others continue; a node cannot tell a slow node from a dead one
Concurrency, transparency, scalability and security follow from these
Examples: IRCTC booking spread over servers, UPI switch talking to many bank hosts

bank.q: Compare message passing with shared memory communication. Explain blocking and non-blocking send and the design consequences of each.
outline: Shared memory needs a common address space; message passing needs only a channel
Message passing has explicit copies, so marshalling and data representation matter
Blocking send: sender waits for buffer space or for the receiver, giving flow control but risking deadlock
Non-blocking send with buffering returns immediately, needs unbounded or bounded buffers and a policy for overflow
Receive may be blocking or non-blocking too; message addressing by name, mailbox or port
Trade-offs: performance, copying cost, simplicity of reasoning

bank.q: Describe remote procedure call step by step. Explain marshalling, stubs, the client-server binding, and the failure semantics of RPC.
outline: Client calls a local stub with the same signature as the remote procedure
Stub marshals arguments into a message, sends it, and blocks on the reply
Server stub unmarshals, calls the real procedure, marshals the result, sends it back
Client stub unmarshals the result and returns it to the caller
Binding: how the client learns the server address and port
Failures: lost request, lost reply, server crash; may-execute, at-least-once, at-most-once semantics
Idempotent operations make retries safe; at-most-once needs duplicate filtering with call identifiers

bank.q: Define the happened-before relation and state the scalar logical clock rules. Prove that a → b implies C(a) < C(b), and show with an example that the converse fails.
outline: Relation defined by program order, message send-receive pairs, and transitivity
IR1: C increments between two events of the same process
IR2: on receive the clock is set to max(local, message timestamp) + 1
Proof by induction along the chain of the relation
Counterexample: two concurrent events can still have unequal scalar timestamps, so concurrency is not detectable

bank.q: Three processes p1, p2 and p3 execute with six messages. Given the event trace, compute the scalar and vector timestamps of every event, and list all pairs of concurrent events.
outline: Apply C = max(C, received) + 1 at each event for scalar clocks
Apply V[j] = max over the two vectors, then increment own entry, for vector clocks
Message carries the sender's timestamp at the send event
Compare vectors: V(a) ≤ V(b) and V(a) ≠ V(b) gives a → b
Concurrency when neither vector dominates the other
Correct step-by-step table of timestamps

bank.q: Explain the Chandy-Lamport snapshot algorithm for FIFO channels. Trace it on a three-process system and show why the recorded state is consistent.
outline: Any process may start by recording its state and sending a marker on every outgoing channel
A process records its state at the first marker it receives and marks that channel empty
Markers on other incoming channels are forwarded after the state is recorded
A channel's state is the sequence of application messages received after the state was recorded and before the marker on that channel
FIFO guarantees no application message can overtake the marker
Proof: for every message either both send and receive are inside the snapshot or neither
Termination: each process records once and each channel contributes finitely

bank.q: Describe how NTP synchronises a client to UTC. Explain offset and round-trip delay computation, strata, and how the client decides which servers to trust.
outline: Client sends a request stamped with its local time, server replies with its own receive and transmit times
Offset θ = ((T2 − T1) + (T3 − T4)) / 2, delay δ = (T4 − T1) − (T3 − T2)
Assumes roughly symmetric path delay; the error is bounded by δ/2
Stratum 0 is the reference clock, stratum 1 servers attach directly, higher strata sync from lower
Selection and clustering algorithms filter falsetickers; the client keeps a set of survivors
Clock is disciplined by slewing (adjusting rate) for small errors and stepping for large ones

bank.q: Design a causal-order multicast for a group of n processes. State the algorithm, and prove that it delivers messages in an order consistent with happened-before.
outline: Each process keeps a vector clock and a delivery queue
Sender increments its own entry and attaches the vector to the message
A message is deliverable when it is next in the sender's sequence and all other entries in its vector are already delivered
Hold undeliverable messages in a queue and re-check on each delivery
Safety: any causally earlier message has a smaller vector entry and is therefore delivered first
Liveness: the message that is next in the required order eventually becomes deliverable
Cost: n counters per message and per process

bank.q: Compare scalar clocks and vector clocks for detecting causality. Prove both directions of the vector clock theorem and state the cost of each scheme.
outline: Scalar: a → b implies C(a) < C(b); the converse is false, so concurrency is invisible
Vector: V(a) < V(b) if and only if a → b
Forward proof by induction over the happened-before chain
Backward proof by contradiction, using the fact that a counter can only grow when its own process takes a step
Concurrency test: neither vector dominates the other
Cost: scalar needs O(1) space and O(1) per message, vector needs O(n) both
Optimisation: direct dependency clocks, and skipping entries for processes that never communicate

bank.q: Compare FIFO, causal and total order broadcast. For each, give an application where the weaker order is enough and one where it is not.
outline: FIFO: messages from the same sender are delivered in send order; different senders may be reordered
Causal: delivery respects happened-before; needed for a reply to arrive after its question
Total: all members deliver in one common order; needed when replicas must agree, e.g. a shared account balance
Total order plus FIFO gives causal order, but causal does not give total
Total order broadcast is equivalent to consensus in the asynchronous crash model
Applications: chat, replicated state machine, distributed lock service

bank.q: Distributed mutual exclusion can be built on Lamport timestamps, on a token, or on quorums. Compare them on message complexity, delay, and tolerance to failure, and state what each assumes.
outline: Timestamp algorithm: request with timestamp, all grant, release; 2(n−1) messages per entry, needs total order on requests
Token ring: 0 messages when idle, 1 to n−1 to pass the token, delay grows with ring size, a lost token stalls the system
Quorum: ask a majority, needs 2 out of 3 or majority sets; tolerates node failure but more messages than a token
Assumptions: FIFO channels, known membership, no byzantine faults
Fairness: timestamp order is fair, token passing may be unfair
Failure handling: election of a new token holder, or lease-based timeouts

bank.q: Explain why a set of independently recorded local states may be inconsistent, and state the exact condition a consistent global state must satisfy. Show how the Chandy-Lamport algorithm satisfies it under FIFO channels.
outline: Local state recording at arbitrary times can record a receive without its send
Consistency condition: for each message, sent is in the snapshot if and only if received is
In-transit messages form part of the global state and must be recorded
Markers cannot overtake application messages on FIFO channels, so a channel's recorded sequence ends exactly at the marker
State the theorem and sketch the proof in both directions
Note the limitation: channel must be FIFO; non-FIFO needs extra bookkeeping

bank.q: A client retries a money-transfer RPC after a timeout and the balance is debited twice. Analyse the cause using RPC failure semantics and propose a fix.
outline: Timeout does not mean the call failed; the server may have executed it
At-least-once semantics with retries gives duplicate execution
Non-idempotent operation: a transfer cannot be repeated safely
Fix: unique request identifier per call and a duplicate filter at the server
Fix: at-most-once protocol with cached replies, or a transaction with commit and abort
Idempotency by design: use a transfer id and make the server reject repeated ids

glossary.def: The property that distribution is hidden from users and programmers, in access, location, migration, replication, concurrency and failure.
The ability of the system to keep working well as the number of users, nodes or messages grows.
The property that interfaces are published so components from different vendors can be added and combined.
An endpoint of a communication channel, identified by an address and a port, over which messages are sent and received.
Encoding arguments and results into a flat byte format so they can be transmitted and decoded on another machine.
An operation that gives the same result and the same effect when executed more than once.
The step in which a client learns the network address and port of the server that offers a required interface.
Storage at the sender, receiver or channel that holds messages until they are consumed.
A single sequential thread of control in a distributed computation; its events form a total order.
A directed path by which messages travel from one process to another; it may reorder or delay messages unless declared FIFO.
For each process, its sequence of events plus, for each message, the send and receive events that pair together.
Delivery order that never places an effect before its cause, i.e. respects the happened-before relation between messages.
A counter driven by a quartz oscillator that approximates real time and is read as a timestamp.
Coordinated Universal Time, the reference time scale to which network clocks are synchronised.
A client asks a time server for its time and adds half the measured round-trip delay to estimate the correct time.
Correcting a clock gradually by running it slightly faster or slower, instead of jumping it, to avoid time going backwards.
The requirement a → b implies C(a) < C(b), which any correct logical clock must satisfy.
The stronger condition that C(a) < C(b) if and only if a → b, achievable only with vector or equivalent clocks.
A control message used by the snapshot algorithm to separate messages already received from messages still in transit.
A property of the whole distributed computation that depends on all local states, such as deadlock or termination.
A service that sends one message to many receivers with a stated ordering and membership guarantee.
The set of processes currently considered part of a group, with agreement on its view among the participants.
A guarantee that membership changes and messages delivered in the same view are seen in the same order by all members.
Deciding that no process is active and no message is still travelling, so the whole computation has finished.
Choosing one process among a group to act as coordinator, agreeing on the choice and handling failures.

textbooks.title: Distributed Systems: Concepts and Design
textbooks.authors: George Coulouris, Jean Dollimore, Tim Kindberg, Gordon Blair
textbooks.pointer: Chapter 6 covers time and coordination, including NTP; chapters 4 and 5 cover IPC and remote invocation.

textbooks.title: Distributed Systems
textbooks.authors: Maarten van Steen, Andrew S. Tanenbaum
textbooks.pointer: Coordination chapter covers physical and logical clocks, mutual exclusion and election; communication chapter covers RPC and message-oriented communication.

textbooks.title: Distributed Computing: Principles, Algorithms, and Systems
textbooks.pointer: Chapters 2 to 5 cover the system model, logical time, causal ordering and global state snapshot algorithms.

textbooks.title: Advanced Concepts in Operating Systems
textbooks.pointer: Part on distributed systems covers logical clocks, vector clocks, global state, mutual exclusion and leader election.
